prompt: Why is laboratory IR spectroscopy generally limited to pure samples of fairly small molecules?

choices.text: Large molecules give too many absorptions to interpret
Large molecules don't absorb infrared radiation
choices.why: They do absorb, but they give so many absorptions that little can be learned.

choices.text: IR radiation breaks large molecules into fragments
choices.why: Absorbed IR energy makes bonds stretch and bend; it doesn't fragment molecules.

choices.text: Small molecules are the only ones with a fingerprint region
choices.why: Large molecules have a fingerprint region too. The limit comes from how complex their spectra are.

explanation: Most organic molecules have dozens of different bond stretching and bending motions, and thus dozens of absorptions. This complexity generally limits laboratory IR spectroscopy to pure samples of fairly small molecules; little can be learned from IR about large, complex biomolecules.

prompt: The fingerprint region of an IR spectrum contains a large number of absorptions. Which vibrations cause them?

choices.text: C–C, C–O, C–N and C–X single-bond vibrations
N–H, C–H and O–H single-bond stretches
choices.why: Those absorb in the 4000 to 2500 cm^−1 region.

choices.text: C≡N and C≡C triple-bond stretches
choices.why: Triple bonds absorb in the 2500 to 2000 cm^−1 region.

choices.text: C=O, C=N and C=C double-bond stretches
choices.why: Double bonds absorb in the 2000 to 1500 cm^−1 region.

explanation: The region below 1500 cm^−1 is the fingerprint portion of the IR spectrum. A large number of absorptions due to a variety of C–C, C–O, C–N and C–X single-bond vibrations occur here.

prompt: Two samples give identical IR spectra. What can you conclude?

choices.text: They are almost certainly the same compound
They are isomers with different structures
choices.why: Different structures give different fingerprint regions. Identical spectra almost certainly mean identical compounds.

choices.text: They share functional groups, but nothing more can be said
choices.why: An IR spectrum is a unique fingerprint of a compound, so identical spectra say much more than that.

choices.text: Nothing, because many compounds share the same IR spectrum
choices.why: An IR spectrum acts as a unique fingerprint of a compound.

explanation: The complexity of an IR spectrum makes it a unique fingerprint of a compound. If two samples have identical IR spectra, they are almost certainly identical compounds.

prompt: A compound has a strong IR absorption at 1710 cm^−1. Which functional group might it contain?

choices.text: A ketone or aldehyde C=O group
An alcohol hydroxyl (O–H) group
choices.why: Alcohol O–H absorbs at 3400–3650 cm^−1 (Table 12.7.1).

choices.text: A nitrile C≡N triple bond
choices.why: Nitrile C≡N absorbs at 2210–2260 cm^−1 (Table 12.7.1).

choices.text: An alkyl bromide C–Br bond
choices.why: C–Br absorbs at 500–600 cm^−1 (Table 12.7.1).

explanation: 1710 cm^−1 lies in the strong carbonyl range of Table 12.7.1, 1670–1780 cm^−1. Carbonyl groups generally absorb at 1680–1750 cm^−1, so the compound might be a ketone or an aldehyde (Exercise 12.7.1a).

prompt: A compound has a strong IR absorption at 1540 cm^−1. Which functional group might it contain?

choices.text: A nitro group, NO2
A ketone C=O group
choices.why: A ketone's strong C=O band is at 1715 cm^−1 (Table 12.7.1).

choices.text: A terminal alkyne
choices.why: A terminal alkyne shows ≡C–H at 3300 cm^−1 and C≡C at 2100–2260 cm^−1.

choices.text: An amine N–H group
choices.why: Amines show N–H at 3300–3500 cm^−1 and C–N at 1030–1230 cm^−1, both of medium intensity.

explanation: Table 12.7.1 lists a strong nitro (NO2) absorption at 1540 cm^−1, so the compound might be a nitro compound (Exercise 12.7.1b).

prompt: A compound shows a strong IR absorption at 1720 cm^−1 and a strong, broad absorption across 2500–3100 cm^−1. What kind of compound might it be?

choices.text: A carboxylic acid
An alcohol that also has a ketone group
choices.why: An alcohol's O–H absorbs at 3400–3650 cm^−1, not across 2500–3100 cm^−1.

choices.text: An aldehyde
choices.why: An aldehyde has a C=O band but no strong, broad O–H band at 2500–3100 cm^−1.

choices.text: A primary amine
choices.why: Amine N–H absorbs at 3300–3500 cm^−1, and amines have no C=O band.

explanation: The 1720 cm^−1 band is a carbonyl C=O, and Table 12.7.1 places the strong, broad O–H band of a carboxylic acid at 2500–3100 cm^−1. Together they point to a carboxylic acid (Exercise 12.7.1c).

prompt: How could IR spectroscopy distinguish ethanol, CH3CH2OH, from its isomer dimethyl ether, CH3OCH3?

choices.text: Only CH3CH2OH shows a strong, broad O–H absorption at 3400–3650 cm^−1
Only CH3OCH3 shows a strong C=O absorption near 1715 cm^−1
choices.why: Neither compound has a C=O group.

choices.text: Only CH3CH2OH shows alkane C–H absorptions at 2850–2960 cm^−1
choices.why: Both compounds have saturated C–H bonds that absorb there.

choices.text: They can't be told apart, because isomers give the same IR spectrum
choices.why: Isomers can contain different functional groups, which absorb at different places.

explanation: CH3CH2OH is an alcohol and has an −OH absorption; Table 12.7.1 puts the alcohol O–H band at 3400–3650 cm^−1 (strong, broad). CH3OCH3 has no O–H group (Exercise 12.7.2a).

prompt: How could IR spectroscopy distinguish cyclohexane from its isomer 1-hexene?

choices.text: Only 1-hexene shows a C=C absorption at 1640–1680 cm^−1
Only cyclohexane shows a C=C absorption at 1640–1680 cm^−1
choices.why: Cyclohexane has only single bonds; 1-hexene is the one with a double bond.

choices.text: Only 1-hexene shows alkane C–H absorptions at 2850–2960 cm^−1
choices.why: Both compounds have saturated C–H bonds that absorb there.

choices.text: Only 1-hexene shows a C≡C absorption at 2100–2260 cm^−1
choices.why: 1-Hexene has a double bond, not a triple bond.

explanation: 1-Hexene has a double-bond absorption: Table 12.7.1 puts alkene C=C at 1640–1680 cm^−1 (and vinylic =C–H at 3020–3100 cm^−1). Cyclohexane has no double bond (Exercise 12.7.2b).

prompt: Acetone, CH3COCH3, and 2-propen-1-ol, H2C=CHCH2OH, are isomers. Which IR evidence tells them apart?

choices.text: Acetone: C=O at 1715 cm^−1; 2-propen-1-ol: O–H near 3500 and C=C near 1660 cm^−1
Acetone: O–H near 3500 and C=C near 1660 cm^−1; 2-propen-1-ol: C=O at 1715 cm^−1
choices.why: That is reversed. Acetone is the ketone, and 2-propen-1-ol is the alcohol with a C=C bond.

choices.text: Both: C=O at 1715 cm^−1; only 2-propen-1-ol: C=C near 1660 cm^−1
choices.why: 2-Propen-1-ol has no C=O group. Only acetone absorbs at 1715 cm^−1.

choices.text: Neither; isomers give the same IR spectrum, so they can't be told apart
choices.why: These isomers have different functional groups, which absorb at different places.

explanation: Identify the functional groups and use Table 12.7.1: acetone has a strong C=O absorption at 1715 cm^−1, while 2-propen-1-ol has an −OH absorption at 3500 cm^−1 and a C=C absorption at 1660 cm^−1 (Worked Example 12.7.1).

prompt: In which region of the IR spectrum do C≡N and C≡C bonds absorb?

choices.why: That region holds N–H, C–H and O–H single-bond stretches.
That is where double bonds (C=O, C=N and C=C) absorb.

choices.text: Below 1500 cm^−1
choices.why: That is the fingerprint region, with C–C, C–O, C–N and C–X single-bond vibrations.

explanation: The IR region can be divided into four parts: 4000–2500 cm^−1 for N–H, C–H and O–H; 2500–2000 cm^−1 for triple bonds (C≡N and C≡C); 2000–1500 cm^−1 for double bonds; and below 1500 cm^−1, the fingerprint region.

prompt: Which bonds absorb in the 4000 to 2500 cm^−1 region of the IR spectrum?

choices.text: N–H, C–H and O–H single bonds
C=O, C=N and C=C double bonds
choices.why: Double bonds absorb from 2000 to 1500 cm^−1.

choices.text: C≡N and C≡C triple bonds
choices.why: Triple bonds absorb from 2500 to 2000 cm^−1.

choices.text: C–C, C–O, C–N and C–X single bonds
choices.why: Those vibrations fall in the fingerprint region, below 1500 cm^−1.

explanation: The region from 4000 to 2500 cm^−1 corresponds to N–H, C–H and O–H single-bond stretching. N–H and O–H bonds absorb in the 3300 to 3600 cm^−1 range; C–H stretching occurs near 3000 cm^−1.

prompt: Thinking of a bond as a spring joining two weights, which order of IR absorption frequency is correct for carbon–carbon bonds?

choices.text: Triple bond > double bond > single bond
Single bond > double bond > triple bond
choices.why: That is reversed. Short, strong bonds vibrate at higher frequency, and triple bonds are the shortest and strongest.

choices.text: Double bond > triple bond > single bond
choices.why: Triple bonds absorb at the highest frequency, C≡C at 2100–2260 cm^−1, above C=C at 1640–1680 cm^−1.

choices.text: All about the same, since each joins two carbon atoms
choices.why: Bond strength and length matter: a short, strong spring vibrates faster than a long, weak one.

explanation: Short, strong bonds vibrate at a higher energy and higher frequency than long, weak bonds, just as a short, strong spring vibrates faster than a long, weak spring. So triple bonds absorb at a higher frequency than double bonds, which absorb higher than single bonds.

prompt: Why do C–H, O–H and N–H bonds absorb at higher frequencies than bonds between C, O and N atoms?

choices.text: Hydrogen is much lighter than C, O and N
Bonds to hydrogen are double bonds
choices.why: C–H, O–H and N–H are single bonds. Their high frequency comes from hydrogen's low mass.

choices.text: Bonds to hydrogen are long, weak bonds
choices.why: Long, weak bonds vibrate at lower frequency, not higher.

choices.text: Hydrogen is heavier than C, O and N
choices.why: Hydrogen is the lightest atom. That is why its bonds vibrate at high frequency.

explanation: In the weights-and-spring picture, C–H, O–H and N–H bonds vibrate at a higher frequency than bonds between the heavier C, O and N atoms. That is why they absorb in the 4000 to 2500 cm^−1 region.

prompt: A compound's IR spectrum shows bands at 1660 cm^−1 and 3100 cm^−1, plus C–H bands at 2850–2960 cm^−1. Which of these compounds fits?

choices.text: 1-Hexene
1-Hexyne
choices.why: 1-Hexyne would show C≡C at 2100 cm^−1 and ≡C–H at 3300 cm^−1.

choices.text: Hexane
choices.why: Hexane has no C=C bond, so it shows no bands at 1660 or 3100 cm^−1.

choices.text: 1-Hexanol
choices.why: An alcohol would show a strong, broad O–H band at 3400–3650 cm^−1, and it has no C=C bond to absorb at 1660 cm^−1.

explanation: 1-Hexene shows a characteristic C=C absorption at 1660 cm^−1 and a vinylic =C–H absorption at 3100 cm^−1, which hexane lacks. 1-Hexyne instead shows C≡C at 2100 cm^−1 and ≡C–H at 3300 cm^−1.

prompt: According to Table 12.7.1, where does the C–Cl bond of an alkyl chloride absorb?

choices.why: That is the C–Br absorption of an alkyl bromide.
That is the C–O absorption of an alcohol.
That is the alkane C–H absorption.

explanation: Table 12.7.1 lists alkyl halide C–Cl at 600–800 cm^−1 and C–Br at 500–600 cm^−1, both strong. Both lie in the fingerprint region, where C–X single-bond vibrations occur.

prompt: According to Table 12.7.1, at what wavenumber does the ≡C–H bond of a terminal alkyne, such as 1-hexyne, absorb?
explanation: Table 12.7.1 lists the alkyne ≡C–H absorption at 3300 cm^−1 (strong). 1-Hexyne shows this terminal alkyne ≡C–H band at 3300 cm^−1 and its C≡C band at 2100 cm^−1.

prompt: According to Table 12.7.1, at what wavenumber does the C=O of an ester absorb?
explanation: Table 12.7.1 lists ester C=O at 1735 cm^−1 (strong), within the general carbonyl range of 1670–1780 cm^−1.

prompt: According to Table 12.7.1, at what wavenumber does the C=O of an amide absorb?
explanation: Table 12.7.1 lists amide C=O at 1690 cm^−1 (strong), toward the low end of the carbonyl range, 1670–1780 cm^−1.

prompt: According to Table 12.7.1, at what wavenumber does the C–H bond of an arene (an aromatic ring) absorb?
explanation: Table 12.7.1 lists arene C–H at 3030 cm^−1, with weak intensity, a little above the alkane C–H range of 2850–2960 cm^−1.

prompt: By how many cm^−1 is the aldehyde C=O value in Table 12.7.1 higher than the ketone C=O value?
explanation: Table 12.7.1 lists aldehyde C=O at 1730 cm^−1 and ketone C=O at 1715 cm^−1: 1730 − 1715 = 15 cm^−1. The exact position within the carbonyl range helps tell carbonyl groups apart.
